curation_status.protected_taxonomy: No target-zone range/learner admission statuses modified; Cuscuta exception preserved; Ipomoea recognized source concept preserved.

project_scope.note: Photo-first Central Texas Convolvulaceae family teaching: real exact-species morning-glory habit, leaves, corolla folds, sepal base and fruit references, including the dodder/Cuscuta leafless parasitic exception. Family science retained.

family_diagnostics.where_to_look_first: LOOK BEHIND THE FUNNEL: five usually FREE SEPALS form the CALYX and persist around the fruit; the FIVE PLICATE/FOLDED fused petals make one funnel-shaped COROLLA. Confirm alternate SIMPLE exstipulate leaves on a twining/trailing stem, and a superior ovary that usually becomes a dry CAPSULE. Do not require leafy green foliage in parasitic dodders (Cuscuta).
family_diagnostics.habit: Often twining or trailing herbs/vines, but not universally.
family_diagnostics.leaves: Typically alternate, simple and without stipules; shape can vary from heart-shaped to hastate or deeply dissected.
family_diagnostics.flower: Usually radial and 5-merous; corolla fused and commonly funnel/bell-shaped with plicate folds or visible mid-petaline bands.
family_diagnostics.fruit: Common leafy morning glories typically mature a CAPSULE that splits to release a few large seeds. The five separate persistent SEPALS remain OUTSIDE the fruit. Seed size and fruit shape can separate superficially similar taxa including the I. lacunosa/cordatotriloba hybrid complex.
family_diagnostics.field_tip: Start with the stem type (TWINS by wrapping vs TENDRIL climbs). Look at ALTERNATE leaves, but remember these may be ENTIRE or PALMATELY LOBED. A PLICATE five-fold COROLLA and FIVE separate persistent SEPALS are the most memorable parts. In genus Ipomoea precise sepal tip/size/hairs outperform 'purple flower + 3 lobes'. Cuscuta is a true leafless/scale-leaved Convolvulaceae exception.

visual_lesson.teaching_order: twining stem and alternate leaf → fused five-fold plicate corolla → five separate pointed sepal calyx under flower → species variability in corolla color and leaf lobes → persistent sepals surrounding fruit → actual ruler and seed evidence → dodder exception
visual_lesson.intro: SEE the actual vine, SPOT the leaf nodes, TURN a flower sideways to find five SEPALS beneath one pleated COROLLA, and FOLLOW the sepals through the fruit stage. Local morning-glories vary hugely in leaf and corolla color. Images here are explicit about what they really show, including which fine macro anatomy is not yet confirmed. The parasitic leafless genus Cuscuta is an important exception to the typical Ipomoea pattern.

steps.title: 1 · Follow the vine and find one leaf node
steps.photo_role: twining vine and alternate leaf arrangement
steps.look_for: VISUALLY REVIEWED: follow the thin green vine running through grass and leaf litter to separate HEART/THREE-LOBED blades. A MORNING-GLORY generally climbs by its TWISTING STEM, not special TENDRILS. Leaves appear one per node (ALTERNATE), on a stalk called the PETIOLE. The scene is a good vine/leaf reference, not evidence of five sepal lengths.
steps.why_it_matters: Teaches habit, nodes, leaf position, twining versus tendrils.

steps.title: 2 · The 'single flower' has a fused, folded corolla
steps.photo_role: five pleats and mid-petal zones of fused corolla
steps.source_credit: (c) Kristin A. Bakkegard, some rights reserved (CC BY-NC), uploaded by Kristin A. Bakkegard
steps.look_for: VISUALLY REVIEWED: two pink-purple morning-glory COROLLAS show bright pale mid-petal sectors separated by darker folded/creased zones. Five fused petals make ONE funnel-shaped COROLLA, not a cluster of five individual corollas. The yellow/white central floral organs are not an aster disk.
steps.why_it_matters: Convolvulaceae petals fuse into a funnel; the pleats are a useful family structure.

steps.title: 3 · Turn the flower sideways to see its five sepals
steps.photo_role: persistent green sepals and hairy calyx at flower base
steps.source_credit: (c) Rodolfo Salinas Villarreal, some rights reserved (CC BY), uploaded by Rodolfo Salinas Villarreal
steps.look_for: VISUALLY REVIEWED: from the SIDE you can see long narrow pointed green SEPALS ascending around the pale corolla tube. White BRISTLY HAIRS surround their bases. Together these five separate SEPALS are the CALYX. Do not mistake the stalk below for an extra sepal. This photo teaches the actual parts, but a mm ruler is still needed to compare precise species values.
steps.why_it_matters: Sepal anatomy is the most informative character for many confusing local morning-glories.

steps.title: 4 · The corolla's color is not a species key
steps.photo_role: blue morning-glory flower front and central throat
steps.source_credit: (c) Douglas Goldman, some rights reserved (CC BY-SA), uploaded by Douglas Goldman
steps.look_for: VISUALLY REVIEWED: the vivid BLUE COROLLA has a pale THROAT and five pleated sectors. Compare the same species' magenta flowers in its separate field images. Color and three-lobed leaves alone do not separate I. hederacea from I. nil; the diagnostic sepals lie HIDDEN UNDER this flower.
steps.why_it_matters: Helps learners reject a seductive but unreliable color-based shortcut.

steps.title: 5 · The small littlebell still has a full morning-glory flower
steps.source_credit: no rights reserved, uploaded by 葉子
steps.look_for: VISUALLY REVIEWED: the tiny lilac-colored funnel is made of fused petals and shows a darker throat. A close-up makes it look enormous, so do NOT visually infer 10–20 mm size without a scale. Its 6–7 mm SEPALS need a separate SIDE VIEW to distinguish it from tie-vine.
steps.why_it_matters: Introduces photographic scale traps: a close-up of a small flower can resemble a large flower.

steps.title: 6 · Whitestar proves the leaves can be lobed
steps.photo_role: small white corolla and a three-lobed leaf
steps.source_credit: (c) Arnan Pawawongsak, some rights reserved (CC BY-NC)
steps.look_for: VISUALLY REVIEWED: one WHITE flower accompanies a deeply lobed leaf with multiple insect-feeding holes. Leaf lobes arise around the petiole base (PALMATE). The feeding holes are insect DAMAGE—not oil glands or extra divisions. Flowers in Convolvulaceae can be white as well as blue/pink.
steps.why_it_matters: Demonstrates leaf variability, small white corolla and the difference between anatomy and herbivory.

steps.title: 7 · Scarlet morning-glory: flower shape varies
steps.photo_role: small scarlet tubular-salverform flowers and broad leaves
steps.look_for: VISUALLY REVIEWED: several small RED/ORANGE trumpets with yellow throats appear along a creeping/twining shoot. Red morning-glory is not an entirely different family. The distinguishing HORNLIKE sepals and a bent-back FRUITING PEDICEL are not proved in this overview.
steps.why_it_matters: Family recognition survives different flower colors and narrow tubes; species diagnosis needs calyx detail.

steps.title: 8 · Palmate leaf divisions are not fern leaves
steps.photo_role: hairy deep palmate leaf and vine stem
steps.source_credit: (c) Ian McFaul, some rights reserved (CC BY)
steps.look_for: VISUALLY REVIEWED: one large, HAIRY, deeply PALMATE leaf has several fingerlike lobes all connected into one BLADE. The surrounding stem is also hairy. This is NOT a compound leaf: the lobes do not each have a separate stalk from the main vine. Lindheimer's giant floral diameter still needs a separate measured bloom.
steps.why_it_matters: Clarifies leaf LOBE versus LEAFLET and shows that not every morning glory has an entire heart-shaped blade.

steps.title: 9 · Morning-glory fruit: sepals can persist after blooming
steps.photo_role: mature fruit surrounded by persistent calyx
steps.look_for: OFFSITE CC BY PHOTO: after the petals fall, the five sepals remain around the small developing/mature CAPSULE. In I. hederacea the narrow tips can retain their curve; their exact length must be measured in a matched fresh sepal or fruit-stage macro. This reference is NOT a physical local file.
steps.why_it_matters: Connects a flower's CALYX to the fruit and explains why seed-bearing material may identify a vine after flowering.

steps.title: 10 · A ten-millimeter fruit teaches scale
steps.look_for: OFFSITE CC BY-SA PHOTO: the ruler/scale demonstrates a 10-mm order of magnitude for the fruit. The fruit is a CAPSULE; the SEPALS persist around its base. The scale is for fruit, not necessarily every sepal tip.
steps.why_it_matters: A physical unit matters: flower/calyx dimensions are difficult to read from portrait photos without a scale.

steps.title: 11 · Critical photo still needed: matched sepal length and shape
steps.photo_role: same-scale five-species outer/inner sepals with confirmed hairs and tips
steps.look_for: Place five fresh labeled calyx profiles of I. triloba, cordatotriloba, hederacea, nil and lindheimeri beside a millimeter ruler. Mark the green CALYX BASE, OUTER SEPAL, INNER SEPAL, long tapered/distal tip and basal pubescence ONLY when actually visible; red/blue flowers, leaf lobing and approximate heights are not substitutes.
steps.why_it_matters: Makes the real taxonomic character learnable by sight and prevents false confidence from front-only portraits.

steps.title: 12 · Critical photo still needed: open a mature capsule
steps.photo_role: capsule ovary, valves and seeds with scale
steps.look_for: Use one mature ripe, vouchered morning-glory CAPSULE and gently expose the few SEEDS. Do not confuse persistent SEPALS outside with parts of the fruit itself. Include seed count, size and pubescence with a scale—especially when comparing lacunosa to possible I. ×leucantha hybrids.
steps.why_it_matters: Seed and fruit anatomy help resolve the difficult white/lavender-flowered tie-vine complex.

steps.title: 13 · Important exception: dodder (Cuscuta)
steps.photo_role: parasitic leafless orange/yellow thread stems and small flowers
steps.look_for: Find a true dodder specimen with thin twining/attaching yellow or orange stems and reduced leaves. Although it belongs within Convolvulaceae, it does NOT have the normal leafy Ipomoea growth form. Needs a licensed local specimen image before learner arrows.
steps.why_it_matters: Stops overgeneralizing the normal leafy, green morning-glory look to the whole family.

steps.title: 14 · Flower-center routing: bindweed, morning-glory, dwarf morning-glory and ponysfoot
steps.photo_role: matched dissected flower centers and stigmas, plus Dichondra ovary, each with millimeter scale
steps.look_for: After confirming the five persistent sepals and fused corolla, inspect the STYLE/STIGMA (pollen-receiving tip): typical Ipomoea has a single capitate (head-like) stigma; local Convolvulus has two slender/linear stigma branches; Evolvulus commonly has two styles forked into four narrow stigma branches; tiny-flowered, mat-forming Dichondra has a deeply two-lobed ovary with styles near its base. These are GENUS ROUTES, not characters to impose on every family member. None of the current front-view Ipomoea photos verifies these hidden stigma/ovary details.
steps.why_it_matters: Gives crew members a structural answer when two plants both have fused five-part flowers, and routes non-twining relatives without relying on petal color.

steps.title: 15 · Family exception and name routing: dodder, Alamo vine and source-name aliases
steps.photo_role: matched Cuscuta thread stem, reduced scale leaf and host contact; Distimake dissectus dissected leaf + flower/fruit
steps.look_for: Cuscuta is parasitic with threadlike shoots, reduced SCALE LEAVES and small clustered flowers; do not require a green leafy vine. Distimake dissectus has strongly dissected leaves but retains the family flower/fruit pattern. Older source name Merremia dissecta is represented by Distimake dissectus, NOT an additional genus/species to install. For a small non-twining groundcover, check Dichondra; for a low silky herb with a small flower, check Evolvulus.
steps.why_it_matters: Covers the remaining source-pool doors and prevents an incorrect 'every bindweed is a heart-leaved twiner' rule or duplicate learner taxon.

comparisons.title: Convolvulaceae vs Apocynaceae
comparisons.rule: Morning-glories commonly have alternate leaves, free persistent sepals, plicate fused corolla and capsule. Milkweed-side Apocynaceae has gynostegium/corona/pollinarium machinery and follicles.

comparisons.title: Convolvulaceae vs Passifloraceae
comparisons.rule: Passiflora climbs with axillary tendrils and has corona + elevated reproductive column; morning-glories usually twine by the stem and lack that architecture.

comparisons.title: Ipomoea vs Cuscuta — exception within Convolvulaceae
comparisons.rule: Morning glories are typically green leafy vines with five-plicate fused corollas; Cuscuta (dodder) is an obligate parasitic genus with little/no green foliage and threadlike host-attached shoots, yet belongs to the SAME family. Do not teach green leaves as universal.

comparisons.title: Ipomoea vs Passiflora and Matelea
comparisons.rule: Ipomoea climbs mostly by TWISTING STEMS, has a five-part fused folded corolla and five persistent separate sepals. Passiflora uses tendrils, has a floral corona and elevated reproductive column. Matelea (Apocynaceae) has a gynostegium/corona and paired follicles instead of a normal Ipomoea capsule.

comparisons.title: Whitestar versus tie-vine hybrid caution
comparisons.rule: I. lacunosa often has a small white flower; I. cordatotriloba often a larger pink-purple flower, but the hybrid I. ×leucantha can be intermediate. Measure sepal, capsule and seeds before overcalling; the hybrid is not an extra canonical learner species.

comparisons.title: Convolvulaceae vs Vitaceae
comparisons.rule: Both may climb, but grape-family vines typically have a TENDRIL or inflorescence opposite a leaf at the node and produce berries. Ipomoea/Convolvulus usually climb by the twining STEM without leaf-opposed tendrils and typically produce dry capsules. Compare matched nodes and mature fruit; don't decide from leaf lobes alone.

visual_lesson.caveat: Some family Convolvulaceae lineages are parasitic (Cuscuta) and do not bear normal leaves. Typical Ipomoea corollas have five pleated sectors, but the family includes other floral forms. Rights/license labels belong to each species source; externally referenced media are not installed images. Captions never assert invisible microscopic parts or measured sepal length without an actual ruler.

previous_steps_before_photo_polish.title: 1 · Follow the vine
previous_steps_before_photo_polish.look_for: Twining/trailing habit with alternate leaves and no stipules.
previous_steps_before_photo_polish.why_it_matters: This gets you into the right family neighborhood before flowering.

previous_steps_before_photo_polish.title: 2 · Look behind the corolla
previous_steps_before_photo_polish.look_for: Five separate or nearly separate persistent sepals.
previous_steps_before_photo_polish.why_it_matters: The sepals are among the best species-level morning-glory characters.

previous_steps_before_photo_polish.title: 3 · Read the folds
previous_steps_before_photo_polish.look_for: A fused funnel/bell corolla with five fold lines or mid-petaline bands.
previous_steps_before_photo_polish.why_it_matters: Plicate corolla architecture is a strong family cue.

previous_steps_before_photo_polish.title: 4 · Expect weird leaves
previous_steps_before_photo_polish.look_for: Deeply divided foliage paired with the same family flower plan.
previous_steps_before_photo_polish.why_it_matters: Stops the learner from requiring heart-shaped leaves.

previous_steps_before_photo_polish.title: 5 · Confirm the capsule
previous_steps_before_photo_polish.look_for: A superior ovary maturing into a dry capsule with a few seeds.
previous_steps_before_photo_polish.why_it_matters: Fruit helps separate Convolvulaceae from milkvines and other twining families.
